clue.text: Speaking first to boy at college, being interrupted by footballer from a London suburb

indicators.note: first here asks for only the opening letter of the word speaking

parts.note: taken as written
Ken is a boy's name

indicators.note: something interrupted has another thing break into its middle, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Eton is the famous English public school, Eton College
a wing is a footballer who plays out on the flank

explanation.surface: A youngster is cut off mid-sentence by a football player from a part of north London.
explanation.walkthrough: Stoke Newington is a district of north London; the place name splits unexpectedly across its two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Stoke Newington is a residential district in the north London borough of Hackney, an example of a suburb.

clue.text: Happening at the same time as I'm in the old Turks' Head getting introductions to every odd, unsuspecting stranger like you

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

parts.note: the sultan was the ruler, or head, of the old Ottoman Turks
taken as written

indicators.note: introductions are the opening letters of each of the following words

explanation.surface: A rambling tale of a stranger meeting the Ottoman ruler at the same moment.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ottoman sultan was the head of the Turks; 'introductions to' takes the initials of the last six words.
explanation.definitionFit: Simultaneous events occur together, at one and the same moment, so this adverb describes concurrence.

clue.text: The Spanish calf's head is thus served up on a plate

indicators.note: in a down clue, served up means the whole string is read from bottom to top

parts.note: el is the Spanish word for the

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: taken as written
so means thus, in this way

explanation.surface: A Spanish dish of calf's head brought to the table on a plate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'served up' reverses the whole string, as a down answer reads upward; 'plate' is the zoological sense, not crockery.
explanation.definitionFit: In zoology an ossicle is a small bony plate or piece, as in the skeleton of a sea urchin.

clue.text: Me acting? I could be hard to make out

indicators.note: could be invites the letters to become something else, a rearrangement

explanation.surface: An actor wonders whether their performance is too obscure to follow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' rearranges the letters of ME ACTING I.
explanation.definitionFit: Something enigmatic is mysterious and puzzling, difficult to understand or interpret.

clue.text: Big Ears with the phenomenal memory is rejoining the panel

definitions.text: Big Ears with the phenomenal memory

indicators.note: rejoining suggests the letters are put back together in a new order

explanation.surface: A large-eared expert with a remarkable memory returns to a quiz panel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejoining' rearranges THE PANEL. Elephants are proverbially said never to forget.
explanation.definitionFit: The animal has huge ears and is proverbially said never to forget, hence the playful description.

clue.text: See 8
Huge Scotsman getting round a gin and tonic? On the contrary

indicators.note: getting round signals one piece surrounding another
on the contrary reverses the stated roles, so the drink goes round the Scotsman

parts.note: G is the usual short form for gin, as in G and T
T is the usual short form for tonic, as in G and T
Ian is a typical Scottish man's name

explanation.surface: A big Scot polishes off a gin and tonic.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, IAN would go round G and T; 'On the contrary' flips it so G and T wrap IAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Giant as an adjective means enormous, of very great size.

clue.text: Senior citizen comes in for a gold stereo!

indicators.note: comes in says the answer sits inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: An elderly person arrives at a shop wanting a golden hi-fi.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes in' points to the run of letters inside 'gold stereo'.
explanation.definitionFit: An oldster is an informal word for an elderly person, a pensioner.

clue.text: Dreadful taste in ties, Mitch and I — all so long ago now

indicators.note: dreadful suggests the letters are badly mangled, a signal to rearrange them

explanation.surface: Someone recalls their and Mitch's terrible taste in neckwear, mercifully long past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dreadful' rearranges all twenty letters of TASTE IN TIES MITCH AND I.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is used when looking back over a long span of years, much as one says something is long ago.

clue.text: Send the wrong way — Maidenhead is straight forward

parts.note: read as maiden head, the head or first letter of maiden
taken as written
direct means straightforward, going straight ahead

explanation.surface: A remark about directions near the Berkshire town of Maidenhead.
explanation.walkthrough: Maidenhead is a town in Berkshire, but here it is split as maiden's head, its first letter M.
explanation.definitionFit: To misdirect is to give someone wrong directions, sending them off course.

clue.text: Check on car time

parts.note: Audi is a German car make

explanation.surface: A garage inspects a vehicle on schedule.
explanation.definitionFit: An audit is an official inspection or examination, particularly of accounts.

clue.text: Greek character with pass coming round when the doctor is off?

indicators.note: coming round means turning about, so the combined string is read backwards

parts.note: mu is a letter of the Greek alphabet
a col is a mountain pass

explanation.surface: A Greek mountaineer visits while the regular physician is away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming round' reverses the whole combined string, not just one piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A locum is a stand-in practitioner covering while the usual doctor is absent, a cryptic description by situation.

clue.text: Man and young woman get little one to do needlework

parts.note: he stands for a man, the male pronoun
Ms is the title used for a woman
titch is British slang for a small person

explanation.surface: A couple persuade their child to take up sewing.
explanation.walkthrough: TITCH is everyday British slang for a small child or person.
explanation.definitionFit: To hemstitch is to sew a decorative hem by drawing out threads, a kind of needlework.

clue.text: Turning aside to affirm money is good

parts.note: to aver is to assert or affirm
tin is old slang for money

explanation.surface: A claim that wealth is virtuous.
explanation.walkthrough: TIN is old British slang for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Averting means turning away or deflecting, as in averting one's gaze.

clue.text: Little girl's teacher called back from wreckage

parts.note: Deb is a pet form of the girl's name Deborah

indicators.note: called back means the word is read in reverse

parts.note: pupils address a male teacher as sir

explanation.surface: A child's schoolmaster is recalled from a crash site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'called back' turns SIR into RIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Debris is scattered remains of something destroyed, which is wreckage.

clue.text: Flake off, dripping round oil spilt in river

indicators.note: in puts one piece inside another

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon

indicators.note: round means one piece surrounds another

parts.note: dripping is fat that drips from roasting meat

indicators.note: spilt suggests the letters are scattered and rearranged

explanation.surface: Fat and oil spilt into a river break up into flakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spilt' rearranges the oil to OLI; dripping is a British cooking fat saved from roast meat.
explanation.definitionFit: To exfoliate is to shed or come off in scales or layers, as skin or bark does.

clue.text: Surrealist painter to urge 10 to play in rapid progression

parts.note: Jean Arp was an artist associated with Dada and Surrealism
to egg someone on is to urge them
the figures 1 and 0 look like the letters I and O

explanation.surface: An artist is pressed to perform at speed.
explanation.walkthrough: '10' is not a cross-reference to 10 across; the digits stand for the look-alike letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An arpeggio is a chord whose notes are sounded one after another in quick succession.

clue.text: Professional losing right for many to anticipate

indicators.note: losing means a letter is dropped from the word
for signals that a new letter takes the place of the old one

parts.note: an expert is a skilled professional
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, i.e. many

explanation.surface: A pro forgoes justice for the masses in the hope of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing' and 'for' together swap the R of EXPERT for C.
explanation.definitionFit: To expect is to look forward to something as likely, which is to anticipate it.

clue.text: Collage a scientist almost accepts quietly

indicators.note: almost means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: Louis Pasteur was the French chemist and microbiologist
P stands for piano, quietly in music

explanation.surface: A scientist almost agrees, softly, to an artwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' drops the final R of PASTEUR; 'accepts' attaches P.
explanation.definitionFit: A paste-up is a layout made by sticking pieces onto a sheet, essentially a collage.

clue.text: Arising from a sci-fi tiff, argue for drawings to be shown in public places

definitions.text: drawings to be shown in public places

indicators.note: arising in this clue means the string of letters is read backwards
from says the answer is extracted from within the words that follow

explanation.surface: A quarrel among science fiction fans spills onto the walls.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'sci-fi tiff, argue' backwards and the answer sits inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Graffiti are drawings or writing scrawled on walls in public places.

clue.text: Have idea about what's popular — think!

indicators.note: about means one piece goes round another

parts.note: an image is a mental picture, an idea
in means fashionable, popular

explanation.surface: A command to consider what is fashionable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have' is a link; the exclamation makes the definition an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To imagine is to form a picture in the mind, to suppose or think.

clue.text: Stance adopted by a Kipling character with a problem

definitions.note: the definition describes a posture; the answer is an adverb describing that stance

parts.note: Kim is the title character of Rudyard Kipling's novel
BO, body odour, is a personal problem

explanation.surface: A literary hero takes up a pose despite a personal difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: BO is body odour.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing with hands on hips and elbows out is the classic stance described by this word.

clue.text: Ask Uncle Henry cunningly to get rid of the chain

indicators.note: cunningly suggests the letters are craftily rearranged

parts.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: A request to a crafty relative to free someone from restraints.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cunningly' rearranges ASK UNCLE H.
explanation.definitionFit: To unshackle is to free from shackles, removing the chain.

clue.text: Revoke article missing from yearbook

indicators.note: missing from signals a piece is removed

parts.note: an annual is a yearbook
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An instruction to cancel because an entry is absent from a yearly publication.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missing from' takes one A out of ANNUAL.
explanation.definitionFit: To annul is to declare invalid or cancel, which is to revoke.

clue.text: Said to have hired the minimum

indicators.note: said to signals a word heard rather than read

parts.note: to have hired a property is to have leased it

explanation.surface: A claim about renting as cheaply as possible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Said to' points to a word that sounds like 'leased'.
explanation.definitionFit: The least is the smallest amount, i.e. the minimum.

clue.text: A form of indulgence that is defended by nothing, on reflection

indicators.note: defended by means surrounded and protected by another piece
on reflection means the word is read backwards, as in a mirror

parts.note: nil means nothing
IE is the abbreviation for id est, that is

explanation.surface: Reflecting on some unprotected indulgence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on reflection' turns the word for nothing to LIN before the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: A lie-in is staying in bed late in the morning, a small luxury or indulgence.

clue.text: Restriction on Soviet aircraft moving elsewhere

indicators.note: on means the restriction is placed after the aircraft

parts.note: the MiG is a Soviet-built fighter jet
a ration is a restricted allowance

explanation.surface: Limits are imposed on Russian jets being relocated.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across answer, 'on' places the restriction after the aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: Migration is the movement of people or animals from one place to another.

clue.text: People say "No Fee" could be the favourite

indicators.note: could be invites the letters to become something else by rearrangement

explanation.surface: A free offer that might well become popular.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' rearranges PEOPLE SAY NO FEE.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a person cherished above all others, the dearest one.
